blocks.title: Catalyst and catalysis
blocks.text: A catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction but remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction; it is often present in a very small amount. The process that takes place in the presence of a catalyst is called catalysis.

The reaction between H2 and O2 to form water is very slow at ordinary temperature but proceeds more rapidly in the presence of platinum; KClO3 decomposes much more rapidly with a small amount of MnO2; and HCl is oxidised to Cl2 in the presence of CuCl2. A catalyst provides a new reaction path with a lower activation energy barrier, so a greater number of molecules can get over the new barrier and the rate increases.

items: Homogeneous catalysis: the catalyst and the reactants are in the same phase and the system is homogeneous throughout, the catalyst distributed uniformly. In the contact process 2SO2(g) + O2(g) gives 2SO3(g) with NO(g) as catalyst, all gases; esters are hydrolysed in the presence of H2SO4, CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O giving CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH, all in solution.

Heterogeneous catalysis: the catalyst and reactants are in different phases, mostly a solid catalyst with gaseous or liquid reactants. Ammonia is oxidised to NO over platinum gauze at 800 degrees C, 4NH3 + 5O2 giving 4NO + 6H2O, the route to nitric acid; unsaturated organic compounds are hydrogenated over finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt, C2H4 + H2 giving C2H6 over nickel at 150 degrees C.

blocks.title: Did you know
blocks.text: Enzymes, nature's catalysts, are usually proteins; they lower the activation energy of biochemical reactions and so speed them up, and their activity depends on pH, temperature and substrate concentration. Vitamins act as catalysts in biochemical reactions, especially as coenzymes that help enzymes work; vitamin K, for example, is needed for blood clotting, and a vitamin deficiency is a cofactor deficiency.

blocks.prompt: Can a catalyst be consumed in a reaction? Is 2SO2(g) + O2(g) giving 2SO3(g) with NO(g) homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysis? Describe the energy profile of an uncatalysed and an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
blocks.explanation: No: by definition a catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end, though it may take part in intermediate steps and be regenerated. With gaseous reactants and a gaseous catalyst the contact process is homogeneous catalysis. Both profiles start at the same reactant level and end at the same product level with the same delta H, but the enzyme-catalysed path has a much lower hump, a smaller activation energy, than the uncatalysed one.

items: A catalyst alters the rate but is unchanged at the end, giving a new path with lower Ea (Pt for H2 + O2, MnO2 for KClO3, CuCl2 for HCl oxidation).

Homogeneous: same phase (NO in the contact process, H2SO4 in ester hydrolysis); heterogeneous: different phases (Pt gauze for NH3 oxidation, Ni for hydrogenation); enzymes and vitamin coenzymes are biological catalysts.
